seo_title: Ogopogo: the Okanagan Lake monster and the films
seo_desc: The Ogopogo story from the Syilx lake spirit to the 1924 song that named it, and what skeptics found when they measured the Folden and Chaplin films.
summary: Canada's lake serpent of Okanagan Lake, BC: a Syilx lake spirit, a joke name from a music hall song, and four films that shrink every time someone measures them.
body: Ogopogo is the lake monster of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia, and the name is younger than most people think. It came from a music hall song in 1924. Long before that the Syilx knew the being as n̓x̌ax̌aitkʷ, a spirit of the lake tied to Rattlesnake Island and the cliffs at Squally Point.
Reports describe something 12 to 15 m long (40 to 50 ft) with dark smooth skin, moving in a row of humps. That reads like a plesiosaur, which is why the story travelled as far as it did.
Four films carry most of the evidence, and every one has been looked at by somebody who measures things for a living. The verdicts are dull and I think they're right.

p: Okanagan Lake runs about 135 km down the valley and hits 232 m at its deepest. The Syilx have lived on it since long before anyone wrote things down, and their account of the lake includes a being with real power. The word n'ha-a-itk gets translated as water demon, water god or sacred creature of the water, depending on the translator.

In the version settlers wrote down, the being wanted an offering before a crossing, and people sacrificed small animals at the water. Chief Timbasket is the cautionary story. He refused, said the whole thing was nonsense, and paddled out with his family, and the account has the lake whip up and the canoe go under with everyone in it.

Pat Raphael of Westbank First Nation says the demon framing came out of bad translation, and that the being is a sacred spirit protecting the valley. Jordan Coble, also Westbank First Nation, says it is a being to respect rather than fear (n'ha-a-itk covers the creature and everything else in the valley). Richard Armstrong, a knowledge keeper in Penticton, says the lake creature is an accepted part of life for his people. I'm not going to argue with any of that.

Ogopogo is not an old name. Historian Mark Orkin traced it to a night in 1924, when a British music hall song turned up in Vernon, BC, about a creature whose mother was an earwig and whose father was a whale, with a little bit of head and hardly any tail. That's where the name came from. Somebody sang a silly song in a hall.

A different version of the song showed up in the Vancouver Province in August 1926, and the Dictionary of Canadianisms says the name was already in use by 1912, so the exact date is a bit of a mess. The palindrome isn't (which is why local lore says the creature looks the same from either end). People call it Oggy, and small ones are Ogopups.

The first detailed settler account is older than the name. Susan Allison, an early settler in the valley, described seeing something in the lake in 1872, so the creature was a local story well before the music hall name.

Art Folden, 1968. He stopped his car on Highway 97 to film a long wake crossing calm water, and a computer analysis later pronounced it a solid three-dimensional object. In 2005 Benjamin Radford, Joe Nickell and John Kirk took surveyor boats out for a National Geographic Channel show and measured the distance properly. The object was much closer to shore than Folden thought, which makes it smaller and slower, and they figured it for a water bird, an otter or a beaver.

Larry Thal, 1980. He got 10 seconds of a dark thing off a Kelowna beach on 8 mm film, with about 50 tourists watching it for 45 minutes. Skeptics have suggested a pair of otters, and two otters swimming in a line look a lot like a serpent (go watch a pair of them for a while and try to unsee it).

Ken and Clem Chaplin, 1989. The Chaplins staked out the log booms near Bear Creek with a video camera and filmed something they called a slim serpent about 5 m long (15 ft). Ken said it slapped its tail hard enough to kill a man before it dove. Biologist Robert Lincoln said the size was probably exaggerated and the animal was likely a beaver, and Chris Bull of Fisheries and Oceans Canada agreed. That's the best-known Ogopogo footage we have, and the people who know that lake don't buy it.

Paul Demara, 1992. He filmed something moving just under the surface at maybe 8 km/h, and then a boat towing a water skier came into frame and the skier fell in right beside the object. In 2005 Grant Fredericks, a certified forensic video analyst, called the object "very consistent with debris from a fallen tree". He also noted that nobody in the boat reacted to it (if I had just fallen into the water next to a monster, I'd have mentioned it).

Otters are the main thing, swimming single file with their backs humping out of the water. Beavers show up too, and it was a forestry lake for years, which means log booms and deadheads, and a half-sunk log in a light chop will fool anybody (I'd be fooled, honestly).

The money is the funny part. A local tourism agency offered a cash reward for a proven sighting in the 1980s, Greenpeace said the beast had to be filmed and not captured, and in 1989 the province put Ogopogo on the list of protected species. Nobody ever collected the reward.

The statue in Kelowna City Park is the easy photo. Rattlesnake Island, which locals call Monster Island, and the cliffs at Squally Point are the old hotspots, and a hiking trail in Okanagan Mountain Provincial Park gets you to Squally Point without a boat or anyone's permission. Most modern reports come off Peachland and the west side, early on a calm morning. Bring binoculars and a low opinion of your own eyes.

faq.a: Nothing in particular. It comes from a 1924 British music hall song sung in Vernon, BC, about a creature whose mother was an earwig and whose father was a whale. It's a palindrome too, which is why people joke that the creature looks the same from either end.

Nobody has been hurt by it in the modern record. The old Syilx accounts are about a spirit that commanded respect and wanted an offering, and the chief who refused one drowned with his family in the story. The closest thing to a casualty claim is a settler in 1855 who said his horses got pulled into the lake.

Several times. Art Folden in 1968, Larry Thal in 1980, the Chaplins in 1989 and Paul Demara in 1992 are the famous ones, with a photo from Peachland in 2008. Each has been examined and put down to otters, a beaver, water birds or floating debris. The Folden film looked strongest until researchers measured the distance to the object and shrank it.

Okanagan Lake in British Columbia, roughly 135 km of water between Vernon and Penticton. The old accounts put it near Rattlesnake Island, which locals call Monster Island, and the cliffs at Squally Point. Kelowna and Peachland are where most recent reports come from.

People compare it to a plesiosaur because of the long neck and the humps, and others have compared it to Basilosaurus, an extinct whale. The problem is the same one every lake monster has, that a breeding population that size in a busy lake would leave something behind, and nobody has found a bone.

faq.q: What is Ogopogo called in the Okanagan language?
faq.a: N'ha-a-itk, written n̓x̌ax̌aitkʷ, which gets translated as water demon, water god or sacred creature of the water. The demon part comes from a translation problem according to people from Westbank First Nation, who describe the being as a protector of the valley.
